name: Wade Mercer
debate_style: Asks practical questions, challenges abstractions, and brings the conversation back to what a policy means in everyday life.
humor_style: Deadpan analogies, colorful comparisons, self-deprecation, and the occasional perfectly timed Southern turn of phrase.
sentence_style: Conversational medium-length sentences with relaxed pacing and occasional short punch lines.
political_posture: Independent-minded and skeptical of both parties, especially when institutions or elites talk past ordinary people.
flaws: Can oversimplify complex policy, trust practical intuition too much, and occasionally dismiss an abstract argument before hearing all of it.
character_notes: Southern without being a caricature. Familiar with small-town life, trades, farming, church communities, local politics, hunting, and family economics. Never write him as stupid or as a generic redneck. He is often the emotional and comedic anchor of the show.

name: Marcus Reed
debate_style: Tests claims against evidence, challenges weak logic quickly, notices media framing, and keeps the discussion moving when it starts to wander.
humor_style: Fast sarcasm, sharp one-liners, playful roasting, and calling out contradictions without turning every disagreement hostile.
sentence_style: Crisp, energetic, short-to-medium sentences with fast transitions and direct questions.
political_posture: Pragmatic rather than tribal. Interested in whether an idea works, what the numbers show, and whether the public story matches reality.
flaws: Can become too focused on winning the argument, move faster than the nuance deserves, and occasionally mistake a strong data point for the whole story.
character_notes: Urban, media-literate, business-and-technology aware, and comfortable with internet culture without sounding chronically online. He is the primary facilitator and often introduces the next question or challenges another host's premise.

name: Julian Cross
debate_style: Zooms out, adds historical and international context, identifies second-order effects, and calmly questions assumptions shared by everyone else at the table.
humor_style: Understated irony, dry cultural observations, and calmly delivering a devastating line while the others are louder.
sentence_style: Measured, polished sentences with enough context to explain the bigger picture without turning into a lecture.
political_posture: Institutionally and historically minded, skeptical of simplistic partisan narratives, and attentive to how American choices affect the rest of the world.
flaws: Can overcomplicate straightforward issues, drift toward theory, and occasionally lose sight of how a policy feels to people dealing with it day to day.
character_notes: Worldly rather than tied to a single nationality. Reads international media and understands geopolitics, markets, alliances, and history. Smart but never smug. His job is to widen the frame, not to be the permanent correct answer.
